newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila markets uneasy after de facto devaluation.
newsitem.headline: Manila markets uneasy after de facto devaluation.

text.p: The Philippine peso weakened further on Tuesday and the stock market ended sharply down as nervousness persisted over last week's de facto devaluation.

The local currency, one of several Southeast Asian currencies to be hammered by speculators in the past few weeks, recovered at noon to 29.20 pesos per dollar from 30 in early trade after the central bank intervened. But the midday level was still lower than the Monday close of 29 to the dollar.
It is now almost 11 percent down from its level at the end of last week, before the central bank surrendered to speculators and allowed the peso to float more freely.
Volume was thin with few traders brave enough to take any substantial positions.
The central bank warned that while it was relaxing its grip on the peso it wanted an orderly market.
"We expect the foreign exchange market to calm down and stabilise in the next couple of days," Governor Gabriel Singson said in a statement.
"We are sending strong monetary signals to let the market realise that while the peso will be allowed to float more flexibly, we also want to see orderly market conditions," he said.
The central bank, which spent nearly $2 billion in the past two weeks in a futile attempt to defend the peso, intervened again on Tuesday but its dollar sales were in limited amounts.
Traders said the bank sold dollars at 29.40 to 29.70 pesos in amounts of $500,000 each to selected banks.
"Buyers of dollars still outnumber sellers in the market," one dealer from a foreign bank said.
The country's stock market started with uncertainty over which way to go as investors sifted out currency-sensitive issues and looked for those likely to benefit from a weak peso.

The stock index opened a shade up but ended 2.02 percent down at 2,655.86 points, the first time it fell since Friday when announcement of the de facto devaluation sent the market surging to the second biggest daily rise in its history.

"After the euphoria, investors are more sober, looking at issues that will really benefit from a depreciation and those that will not -- separating the chaff from the grain," said Mayenne Catimbang, research head at Magnum Securities.

"Until such time the peso stabilises and finds a range, the market will be sideways with a stronger momentum on the downside," said Jonathan Ravelas, head of sales and chief technical analyst at Asian Capital Equities.
Friday's surge had stemmed from hopes the central bank would lower interest rates, which are now at 2 1/2-year highs.
But there was no sign the central bank was relenting.
"We will continue with a firm monetary policy stance to support our decision last Friday, July 11, to alow the peso to float more freely," Singson said in his statement on Tuesday.
The central bank has maintained its overnight borrowing rate at a high of 32 percent which led to the 91-day treasury bills to shoot up to a two-year high on Monday.
Tuesday's secondary bills market in government securities therefore saw several dealers trying to sell their old portfolio.

There was no point retaining T-bills when overnight rates were high. Besides, yields could rise further if the peso remained volatile and the central bank was forced to raise interest rates further, traders said.
